title: The Orthodox Church
hookLine: icons, incense, the Divine Liturgy and becoming like God by grace

cards: Around the year 987, an old chronicle from Kyiv says, Prince Vladimir sent envoys out to see how different peoples worshiped. Back from Constantinople, from the great church of Hagia Sophia, they could hardly describe it.

They said, more or less: we didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth. We only know that God dwells there among people. The gold, the singing, the incense rising through light from high windows.

Soon after, Vladimir was baptized, and with him the people of Kyiv. Step inside an Orthodox church today, Greek, Russian, Romanian, Serbian, Ukrainian, and some visitors still describe what those envoys described.
Candles flickering before painted faces. People kissing pictures. Many standing.

teach.b: Orthodoxy is Greek: orthos, right or straight, and doxa, which means both belief and glory. So: right belief, and right worship, or praise.
Orthodox Christians would say you can't separate the two: what you believe is how you pray.

teach.h: A FAMILY OF CHURCHES, ONE FAITH.
teach.b: The Orthodox Church is a family of self-governing churches, the patriarchates of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, and the churches of Russia, Greece, Romania, Serbia and more, sharing one faith and one communion, with no single head.

Its main service is the Divine Liturgy, most often the one named for Saint John Chrysostom, sung almost entirely. Icons fill the church: Christ, Mary, the saints. Kissing an icon isn't worshiping wood and paint.

teach.h: THE HONOR PASSES TO THE ONE SHOWN.
teach.b: A council in 787 said the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love. And the goal of it all has a surprising name: theosis, becoming like God.
It's rooted in a line from Second Peter, that we might be "partakers of the divine nature." Early church fathers went further: God became human so that humans might share God's life.
The Orthodox are careful here: not by nature, as if people turn into gods, but by grace, the way iron left in a fire glows with the fire's heat while staying iron.
This week's arc: one church, then many; the councils; the ancient churches of Africa and Asia; the road east; 1054; and now worship as heaven on earth.

how: Orthodox Christians often keep an icon corner at home with a small lamp, cross themselves and kiss the icons when they enter church, and stand through a Divine Liturgy that is sung from start to finish.

o: a strict, old-fashioned faith that resists change
the official religion a government picks for all
right belief and right praise, from two Greek words

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the honor passes to the one shown

s: Orthodox Christians worship the wood and paint of icons
a council in 787 said the honor given an image passes to the one it shows.
the Orthodox Church has one single head, like a pope
it's a family of self-governing churches sharing one faith and communion.
doxa means both belief and glory
so Orthodoxy is right belief and right praise.

games.q: you walk into an Orthodox church and see an old woman kiss a painting of Christ. what is she doing, in the church's own words?
o: honoring Christ, the one the painting shows.
games.why: the council of 787 taught that honor given to an icon passes to the one it shows, like kissing a photo of someone you love.

practice: Light a candle before a holy picture, or a photograph of someone you love; if you can't light a flame, picture one. Look at the face, and let the honor you feel pass through the picture to the person it shows.
If you pray, pray the way Orthodox Christians do before icons, silently, simply, eyes open; if you don't, just keep looking with love.

wordCard.voice: Orthodoxy. Right belief and right praise, from the Greek orthos and doxa. The church of icons and the Divine Liturgy.
